title: More PWM transfers more power

takeaway.text: More burst-enable PWM increases average energy transfer; the V2 secondary load points show power increasing with current.

visible_content.condition: V2 · direct secondary load before USB-C PD · 240 V AC, 50 Hz

visual.layout: Two vertically stacked, horizontally aligned plots dominate the slide. Both use the same linear secondary-current axis, extent 0–11 A, and aligned tick positions. The upper plot shows secondary power from 0 to 150 W; the lower shows secondary voltage from 0 to 30 V. Show the shared current-axis label below the lower plot and the test condition above. Place each labeled callout adjacent to its corresponding marker, without obscuring the data or another label. Distinguish the two highlighted current points with consistent marker styling across both plots. No legend is needed.
visual.chart_style: Plot all seven measured voltage/current pairs and the corresponding calculated power/current pairs as discrete markers joined in measurement order by straight line segments. Do not smooth, extrapolate, or use a dual axis. Use ordinary consistent measured-result styling and editable labels; preserve clear whitespace around the two endpoint callouts.

speaker_notes: After the tank changes, an electronic load was connected directly to the V2 secondary, before the USB-C PD stage. The burst-enable PWM acts like a throttle: a greater enabled fraction gives the converter more switching time and increases average energy transfer. The two plots show the resulting secondary voltage and calculated power against load current. At 1.86 amperes, the load received 48.68 watts at 26.14 volts. At 4.29 amperes, the voltage was 20.07 volts and the power was 86.17 watts. At the highest current of 10.01 amperes, the voltage was 13.69 volts and the power reached 137.08 watts. The change in secondary voltage across the sweep was expected.
transition: The same load sequence also shows where heating remained and guides the next circuit changes.

facts: All seven current, voltage and calculated power values reproduce the CSV exactly. Power is voltage multiplied by current; displayed callouts are rounded to two decimal places.
